(1) The `exclude_columns` argument did not take effect: I passed it twice, as a JSON array and as a comma-separated string, and both runs returned n_columns_excluded=0, excluded_columns=[] and byte-identical output (467,991 characters). So the verdict was computed with SUBJECT ID, GROUP code, SEX and all six date columns INCLUDED -- columns that repeat across patients by design (rulebook rule 11a). (2) The flagged share is a saturation signature, not a duplication signature: 2,260 pairs out of the 3,655 possible pairs among 86 patients is roughly 62% of the entire pair space. A genuine copy-paste artifact is rare and localised; a detector firing on the majority of all pairs is describing the data type. (3) The sheet is a wide table of bounded low-cardinality cognitive scores (MoCA, digit span forward/backward, Hamilton depression and anxiety totals) alongside z-score transforms of those very columns, so every raw-score collision is counted again in its derived column (rule 11b, 11c). Notably the tool found ZERO repeated column sequences and ZERO repeated high-precision values -- the two signals that would indicate real copy-paste. No duplication finding is asserted against this paper.

STATED CAVEAT, which the editorial stage must carry: the paper did not use either procedure. It used Nnpar 1.0, a non-parametric MULTIVARIATE sample-size method that pools information across 10 correlated outcome scales at rho=0.4, and such a method can legitimately require fewer subjects than a univariate test. So this is a finding that the published power statement cannot be reproduced from the parameters given, not a demonstration that it is arithmetically wrong. Mitigating context: the paper repeatedly concedes the point itself -- 'Given the low sample size of the trial that would inherently lead to the low power of reported analyses' -- so the underpowering is disclosed rather than hidden.

findings.title: Per arm randomised ns never reported (Results, paragraphs 1 and 4)
findings.description: A three-arm parallel-group RCT reported under CONSORT never states how many patients were randomised to each arm, nor the per-arm ITT or per-protocol sizes (CONSORT items 13a and 16). The only per-arm ns anywhere are 24/20/20 for the 64-patient complete-case subset used in the composite analysis. This has a direct forensic cost: without per-arm denominators, most percentage- and proportion-based checks (GRIM on any per-arm rate, reconstruct_2x2 on the adverse-event distribution) cannot be run at all, and a reader cannot judge whether allocation was balanced. It also means the 22 ITT patients dropped from the composite analysis (26% of the ITT set) cannot be located by arm.

What can be stated from reading alone: the paper performs at least 48 omnibus tests (22 ITT + 22 PP in the annex, plus 2 composite and 2 safety in the text) and 132 supplementary pairwise comparisons. Bonferroni is applied only WITHIN each outcome's three pairwise contrasts; nothing corrects across the 22 outcome-by-timepoint families or across the two analysis populations. Two of the 22 ITT omnibus tests fall below 0.05, which is close to the 1.1 expected by chance -- so the multiplicity burden here most likely argues AGAINST reading the significant Digit Span Backward result as real, and the editorial stage should weigh it that way rather than as an additional problem. Separately, the Results state that 'no further hypothesis testing was performed', which is contradicted by the 176 tests reported in the supplement.
